 She Inherited Her Partner’s $1.1 Million House After 17 Years Together. His Will Cannot Give Her a Social Security Survivor Benefit
 A will handed her a mortgage-free home worth over a million dollars, but a completely separate body of law controls what she never thought to ask about before her partner died.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 6, 2026, 9:02pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A will transfers property but cannot grant Social Security survivor benefits, which require legal marriage of at least nine months.
 Missing a survivor benefit can cost an unmarried partner $19,200 per year, which adds up to roughly $384,000 over 20 years before cost-of-living raises.
 Common-law marriage recognized by your state can unlock survivor benefits, so filing a claim with supporting evidence is worth attempting.

 Imagine a woman who spent 17 years with a partner whom she loved but never married. When he dies, his will leaves her his mortgage-free home, worth about $1.1 million. His three children inherit $600,000 in other assets, and now they’re challenging her claim to the house.
 The house fight gets the attention. The subtler loss is his monthly Social Security check. Long-term couples who never married often find this out too late. One parent asked online whether a son’s girlfriend of 10 years, who had lived with him for eight years, could be treated as a spouse for benefits. In most cases, the answer is no.
 A Will Can Hand Over a House, but Only Marriage Unlocks His Benefit
 A will controls property. Federal law decides who can collect Social Security on a worker’s record, and a will can’t add anyone to that list. The inheritance dispute and her survivor eligibility are two separate legal questions. She could win the house outright and still get nothing extra from Social Security.
 To collect as a surviving spouse, she generally must be at least 60, or 50 to 59 with a disability, and have been married for at least nine months before his death. Seventeen years of living together doesn’t satisfy that requirement by itself. A legally recognized marriage lasting nine months generally would, although exceptions to the duration rule exist.
 There is one opening. Social Security recognizes a common-law marriage as a valid marriage if it meets the requirements of the state where the couple lived. It also accepts some valid non-marital legal relationships. A handful of states still recognize common-law marriage. If they lived in one of them and presented themselves as married, for example by filing joint tax returns or calling each other husband and wife, she should apply and let the agency decide.
 What the Missing Survivor Check Costs Her
 A widow who claims at her survivor full retirement age (FRA) can receive up to 100% of her late spouse’s benefit, depending on his claiming history. Suppose he collected $3,000 a month and her own benefit is $1,400. If she qualified for the full survivor benefit, her total monthly payment would rise to $3,000. Without that eligibility, she stays at $1,400.
 That gap is $19,200 a year. Over 20 years it comes to $384,000, before cost-of-living raises that could make the difference even bigger. For perspective, Social Security estimates the average widow or widower living alone will receive $2,005 a month in January 2027.
 Her own claiming age now matters more than it would for a married survivor. Without a larger survivor check to fall back on, waiting until 70 can raise her monthly benefit if she hasn’t claimed yet. Continued work could also help if new earnings replace lower-paying years in her Social Security record.
 Why a $1.1 Million House Can Still Leave Her Short Each Month
 A paid-off house cuts her housing costs, but it doesn’t pay property taxes, insurance or the furnace repair. If her own benefit can’t cover those bills, she may have to dip into savings, borrow against the property or consider selling.
 Federal tax law helps here. Inherited property generally gets a new tax basis equal to its fair market value when the owner dies. If she sells soon after the estate closes, her taxable gain may be small. That matters because a large one-time gain can raise Medicare premiums two years later. Under the 2026 rates, a single filer with income above $109,000 pays at least $284.10 a month for Part B, up from the standard $202.90.
 Two Moves Worth Making Before Assuming the Door Is Closed
 Test the relationship against your state’s rules. Collect joint tax returns, shared accounts, insurance forms and anything else showing the two of you held yourselves out as married. Then file a claim. If the agency denies it, the answer will be in writing and you can appeal. If you never apply, you never find out.
 Plan your budget on your own benefit alone. Pull your earnings record and decide when to claim based on that one check. If the house ends up sold or tied up in court, a larger lifetime benefit is the income nobody can contest.
 For couples who are both still living, the lesson is simpler. A short trip to the courthouse can protect the surviving partner’s income in a way no will can.
 Every family’s facts differ. The state you lived in, your ages and the details of your work histories can all change the answer, so have a benefits representative and an estate attorney review your situation before you rely on any of this.
